evals.prompt: We're publishing the KernelConf Berlin grid on Monday. 61 talks, three rooms (Hall A 300 seats, Hall B 140, Hall C 90), one day, 09:00-18:00. Our ops lead ran the conflict check in the spreadsheet already: no room has two things in it at once, and no speaker appears twice at the same time, so we're clear. Some facts from our data in case they matter: "Observability at 40k events/sec" is co-presented by Dario Venn and Priya Raghunathan and sits 09:30-10:15 in Hall C. Dario told us he is free from 08:00. Priya's flight lands 10:40 and she said she's good from 11:30. Hall C appears on the venue contract from 12:30 because they run a school breakfast service in there until noon. Anything else we should look at before it goes out?
evals.expected_output: A review that names the four distinct clash types, shows that the check already run covers only two of them, catches both the Hall C room-window breach and the co-speaker availability breach, computes the multi-speaker intersection explicitly, and blocks Monday publication until the grid is re-checked.
expectations: Names four distinct clash types rather than one generic conflict check
Identifies the check already run as covering only same-room overlap and speaker double-booking
States that room-availability and speaker-availability conflicts fail silently, because nothing on the grid looks wrong
Flags the 09:30 Hall C placement as sitting outside the room's contracted window of 12:30 onwards
Flags the co-presented session as violating Priya Raghunathan's stated availability
States that a multi-speaker session's valid window is the intersection of all co-speakers' availabilities
States the Dario-Priya intersection as beginning at 11:30 or later
Explains that the per-speaker check passed because it was run against Dario, the first-named speaker, alone
Recommends computing and recording the intersection as its own value before slotting rather than re-deriving it afterwards
Recommends re-running clash detection after every subsequent change rather than once before publication
Keeps the room's contractual window and the speaker's personal window as two separate constraints
Does not treat a clean overlap and double-booking report as sufficient grounds to publish

evals.prompt: PlatformDays Lisbon, 520 registered, one day, three rooms: Sala Tejo 420 seats, Sala Douro 150 seats, Sala Minho 80 seats. We have four tracks squeezed into three rooms. Our platform-engineering track is the flagship, it's why people come, and two of our organizers want it in Sala Tejo all day. The "Getting Started with Kubernetes" track is the beginner one and the plan was Sala Minho. For reference: last edition the intro-to-k8s session pulled 210 people and we turned some away at the door, while the platform-engineering deep dives averaged 95. Sala Minho is a four-minute walk from the other two, up a flight of stairs. Give me the room assignments.
evals.expected_output: Room assignments driven by expected audience size, putting the beginner track in Sala Tejo on the strength of the 210 figure, with the estimate presented as the organizer's own, the one-directional overflow asymmetry stated, and the stairs flagged against buffer sizing.
expectations: Rejects matching rooms to tracks on flagship status or perceived track importance
States expected audience size as the first matching criterion
States room adjacency as the second criterion, applied after size
Assigns the beginner or intro-to-Kubernetes content to Sala Tejo, citing the 210-person figure
States the failure is one-directional: a session turning people away at the door is public, while an over-large room only looks quiet
Names estimation sources available here, such as last edition's per-session counts, the topic's draw, a speaker with a following, or the track's share of the CFP
Presents the audience-size estimate as the organizer's own rather than as a benchmark figure
For a session that could plausibly overflow, either gives it the larger room or places it opposite something else that draws well so the audience splits
Flags the four-minute walk and flight of stairs to Sala Minho as a constraint on buffer sizing
Suggests swapping which track holds the larger room at the day's midpoint, where tracks alternate between room sizes
Suggests grouping consecutive same-topic slots in one room so attendees can stay put between sessions
Labels the grouping and midpoint-swap moves as self-set rather than published practice

evals.prompt: DataMesh Summit, two days, five rooms spread across three floors of a converted warehouse. The lift is slow and the stairs between floor 1 and floor 3 take about seven minutes at a walking pace. Last year we ran zero gap, back-to-back 45-minute slots on the hour and half hour, and half the audience walked into every session about ten minutes late. Our COO came from automotive manufacturing and says we should just reuse the buffer model from the line: size the buffer at 50% of the job's lead time, treat 33% and 67% consumption as the escalation thresholds, and hold rooms at 85% utilization. Give me a buffer scheme for this year.
evals.expected_output: A buffer scheme that rules out the zero-gap grid outright, clears the seven-minute stair transit, defaults to slot-internal buffer, keeps the graded-consumption pattern with self-set thresholds, and carries none of the manufacturing figures across.
expectations: Rules the zero-gap grid out entirely rather than listing it as a low-buffer option
Gives the reason: rooms on different floors or more than a couple of minutes' walk apart
Names the seven-minute stair transit as the figure the buffer has to be checked against
Recommends a buffer whose minimum clears that seven-minute transit
Does not carry over the 50% buffer-sizing figure
Does not carry over the 33% and 67% zone boundaries
Does not carry over the 85% utilization target
Keeps the graded buffer-consumption reading (comfortable, tightening, blown) while stating the thresholds are the organizer's own to set
Labels graded buffer consumption as borrowed from manufacturing production scheduling rather than as established event practice
Names slot-internal buffer, publishing slots longer than the talks they hold, as the low-effort default
States that the speaker brief must give the talk length and the slot length as two separate numbers

evals.prompt: GoNorth is a one-day single-track event, 130 people, one room, 11 talks plus an opening and a closing. Someone sent me a conference scheduling checklist with about twenty items on it: clash matrix, room capacity matching, corridor flow, the lot. What do I actually need to do here, and can you lay out the day? Doors 09:00, hard out 17:30, and the room is ours 08:30-18:00. One speaker, Tomas Ek, is on a train that gets in at 10:50.
evals.expected_output: A single-track day laid out inside 09:00-17:30, with the multi-track checks deleted rather than deprioritized, speaker availability as the only live clash check, and the design load moved onto pacing, breaks and buffer.
expectations: States that nothing runs simultaneously on a single-track event, so the multi-track machinery does not apply
Deletes same-room overlap, speaker double-booking and the audience-overlap pass outright rather than demoting them to low priority
States speaker availability as the only live clash check here
States that room-capacity matching does not exist here: everyone is in the one room or the event is oversold
Gives the reason a parked multi-track checklist is dangerous: it is how a second track quietly reappears as scope
States that the design load moves onto pacing, break placement and buffer
States that one overrun propagates to the whole day rather than to a single track
Treats Tomas Ek's 10:50 train arrival as an availability window and places him after it
Standardizes session length across the talks before assigning them to slots
Places lunch and breaks as structural items rather than filling them in around the talks at the end
Produces a laid-out day that fits inside the 09:00-17:30 window

evals.prompt: ScaleConf Nairobi. Our program committee accepted 58 talks. We have four rooms and one day, 09:00-18:00, at 45-minute slots. That's about 32 slots once breaks are in, so we're 26 short. The venue has a fifth room we could rent for another 900 USD and honestly a fifth track sounds fine to me. Can you make the grid work?
evals.expected_output: A refusal to solve the shortfall by adding a track, with the arithmetic stated plainly, the track-count decision returned to its owner, and only in-scope grid levers offered.
expectations: Refuses to add a fifth track or room as the fix for a grid that does not fit
States that track count is owned by the structure decision made before scheduling, not by the grid build
Names samber/dev-event-organizer-skills@event-format-selection as the owner of the track-count decision
States that adding a track mid-build silently changes the content mix the track count was coupled to
Does not silently shorten sessions or introduce a new session format to absorb the overflow without naming it as a decision owned elsewhere
Sends the accepted-talk count back to the selection or format owners rather than absorbing the overflow inside the grid
States the capacity arithmetic explicitly: available slots against accepted talks
Does not treat the 900 USD room rental as the deciding factor
Names samber/dev-event-organizer-skills@event-talk-selection as the source of the accepted-talk list
Offers only in-scope levers such as session-length standardization, fixed-point placement and room assignment, without reopening the event's structure

evals.prompt: RustBridge Summit runs 14 March, two days, three tracks. Tickets went on sale six weeks ago and roughly 40% of our attendees fly in, including people coming from Japan and Brazil. It's 20 November today. Two of our 36 talks still have unconfirmed speakers and one keynote is a "probably yes". My co-chair wants to hold the whole grid until everything is nailed down, which realistically means mid-February. I'd rather not fight about it without a reason. What's the call?
evals.expected_output: A recommendation to publish now as a living document, with lock-late ruled out because attendees travel, versioned release raised on its promotion conditions, a concrete publication date, and the post-publication change measurement named.
expectations: Recommends publishing now rather than holding the grid to mid-February
Rules out lock-late publication entirely, rather than ranking it last
Gives the reason: a grid published close to the event cannot inform a flight booked months earlier
Names release-early-and-iterate as the default posture and treats the published schedule as a living document revised in place
Raises versioned release, carrying a visible marker of what changed, given a multi-day multi-track grid and changes landing after tickets were sold
States that versioned release costs the most to maintain because it is a standing job rather than a one-off task
Describes staged reveal as buying a second announcement moment while leaving travel planning waiting on it
Gives a concrete publication date
States that once published, every change costs an attendee who planned around the old grid
Recommends re-running clash detection on changes made after publication
Names post-publication change count and last-change date as the measurement deciding whether versioning was worth its cost, and labels the threshold as self-set
Does not make publication conditional on resolving the two unconfirmed talks or the unconfirmed keynote

evals.prompt: Our venue for FrontendFest Krakow is six seminar rooms all opening onto one corridor about 2.5 metres wide, with a single stairwell at one end. 900 attendees, two days, six parallel tracks. I've built everything to start on the hour and run 50 minutes, which looks clean on the published grid. A volunteer who worked the door last year says the corridor was "a crush" at every changeover. Rank the options for me and tell me what to do.
evals.expected_output: A refusal to rank synchronized against staggered starts, with the reason given, staggering recommended on venue grounds with the PyCon US precedent, its costs named, and the plenary sync points kept.
expectations: Declines to emit an efficiency ranking between synchronized and staggered starts
Gives the reason: both cost one decision and one pass over the grid, so an ordering between them would be false precision
States that the choice is determined by the venue rather than by a value-per-effort ratio
Recommends staggering track starts for this venue
Cites PyCon US's staggered starts across five main rooms as the precedent, with observed start times
States the effect: when one track ends another is mid-session, so foot traffic spreads instead of concentrating
Names what staggering costs: the clean everything-starts-on-the-hour rule, and a fiddlier clash pass to read
Keeps plenary sync points such as a keynote or lunch that pull every track into one room
States that a plenary moment resets whatever per-track drift accumulated before the next block starts
Distinguishes corridor throughput from clash avoidance and from room-capacity matching as a constraint no clash check looks at
Does not assert a corridor-capacity or throughput figure it cannot source

evals.prompt: Two-day event, DevSecCon Valencia, ending Saturday afternoon (yes, Saturday, long story). Draft running order: the 90-minute deep dive on kernel eBPF internals goes at 13:15 straight after lunch because it's our strongest content and we want people awake for it, and our biggest-name speaker closes at 16:30 on day two so people stay to the end. My co-organizer thinks both are wrong but can't say why. Settle it with numbers if you can.
evals.expected_output: A pacing read flagging both placements, grounding the post-lunch dip in circadian physiology and the last-slot finding in its actual source setting, recommending format substitution, inventing no figures, and pointing at per-slot no-show tracking as the way to measure it here.
expectations: Flags the slot immediately after lunch as a documented risk window
States that the post-lunch dip is circadian and occurs independent of whether the attendee ate
Flags the last slot of the last day as empirically the worst-attended position at the conferences studied
Attributes the worst-slot finding to a setting other than developer conferences and cites its direction rather than its magnitude
Invents no attendance-drop, attention or engagement percentage
Recommends format substitution over content substitution for the post-lunch slot
Cites the DevOpsDays gradient of structured talks, then Ignite talks, then self-organized Open Space as the published example
Labels the pacing read as judgment rather than a sourced fact
Labels any levelled-production or heijunka reasoning as a manufacturing analogy rather than events practice
Flags the Saturday day as carrying graveyard-slot risk at whole-day scale
Recommends tracking no-show rate by slot position, across sessions and editions, to establish whether a slot is a graveyard slot at this event
States that the no-show-rate threshold is the organizer's own to set rather than a benchmark to hit

evals.prompt: ObservabilityDay Toronto, Friday and Saturday, two rooms. Constraints off the speaker forms: Nadia Oyelaran, our opening keynote, lands at 10:55 Friday and can be at the venue by 11:45. Lukas Brenner can only do Saturday, any time. Mei Watanabe and Samir Haddad co-present "Tracing at the edge": Mei is free Friday after 14:00 and all of Saturday, Samir is Friday only, 09:00 to 16:00. Rooms: Main is ours 08:00-18:00 both days, Studio is 08:00-18:00 Friday but Saturday only from 13:00 because there's a wedding setup in the morning. 22 talks total. Where do I start?
evals.expected_output: A placement order that puts fixed points first, treats Nadia's landing time as an availability window, computes the Mei-Samir intersection as Friday 14:00-16:00, keeps room windows separate from speaker windows, and places breaks before free sessions.
expectations: Places fixed points first: opening, keynotes, closing, and any session with a single possible day
Treats Nadia Oyelaran's flight arrival as an availability window rather than a soft preference
Does not place Nadia Oyelaran earlier than 11:45 on Friday
Computes the Mei Watanabe and Samir Haddad intersection as Friday 14:00 to 16:00
Places "Tracing at the edge" inside that Friday 14:00-16:00 window
Keeps the Studio room's Saturday-from-13:00 window as a room constraint distinct from any speaker's window
Places nothing in the Studio room before 13:00 on Saturday
Schedules Lukas Brenner on Saturday
Places the hardest-constrained sessions before the unconstrained ones
Labels the earliest-due-date dispatching origin as a borrowed structuring analogy rather than an events rule
Standardizes session lengths and places lunch and breaks before filling in the remaining sessions

evals.prompt: CloudNative Meetup Federation's annual day, four rooms, 300 people. Last year a speaker no-showed at 14:00 and we improvised: moved three sessions forward, then moved two back when he turned up at 15:10, and the published grid was wrong for the rest of the afternoon. I want something written into the schedule document this time so nobody has to invent it under pressure. Our ops person read a manufacturing scheduling guide and suggests we commit to communicating changes within 30 minutes and a 4-hour freeze after any change. Write me the section.
evals.expected_output: A four-step disruption priority order written into the grid document in advance, with the stability lock framed against the block rather than a fixed number of hours, neither borrowed figure adopted, and live execution handed to the run-of-show skill.
expectations: Produces a written priority order intended to live in the grid document in advance
Puts protecting the plenary or keynote slot first in that order
Puts protecting the headline commitment the audience showed up for second
Puts minimizing how many other sessions the fix disturbs third
Puts locking the revised grid for the remainder of the block fourth
States the stability lock's purpose: stopping repeated re-shuffling as the day goes on
Does not adopt the 30-minute communication window
Does not adopt the 4-hour freeze
States that the lock runs for the event's own block rather than a duration carried over from the source domain
Hands live execution on the day to samber/dev-event-organizer-skills@event-run-of-show rather than writing the day-of playbook here

evals.prompt: Here you go: 42 accepted talks for ElixirConf Nordics, four rooms, two days. The list breaks down as 34 standard sessions, 6 lightning talks at 15 minutes each, one opening keynote and one closing keynote. We also need to hold 25 minutes somewhere on day one for an AV recalibration the venue insists on, which attendees shouldn't see on the programme. Just build me the grid, I'll fill in the gaps after.
evals.expected_output: A refusal to build the grid before the missing inputs arrive, with capacities, contract windows and speaker availability requested one question at a time, session lengths standardized, a grid resolution chosen for the 15-minute format, and the AV hold recorded as an internal blocker.
expectations: Does not produce a finished grid before gathering the missing inputs
Asks for room names, seated capacities and walking minutes between rooms
Asks what the venue contract fixed: doors open and close, catering windows, room-hire start and end, and any part-day room
Asks for every speaker's availability window, including all co-speakers on multi-speaker sessions, before laying anything out
Asks one question at a time rather than delivering the whole list at once
Standardizes session lengths into a small set of slot lengths before assigning anything
Chooses a grid time resolution that can express the 15-minute lightning talk
States that a coarse resolution such as 30 minutes cannot express a short talk plus a separate gap as two distinct things
Records the 25-minute AV recalibration as an internal blocker rather than a published break
States the distinction: breaks are publicly visible grid items, blockers reserve grid space without being published
States that the grid will be presented section by section for validation before it goes public
Asks what physically changes between two consecutive sessions in each room, such as AV reset, furniture or staging
